claim: Long-term balancing selection acting on mating types or sex-determining genes is expected to lead to the accumulation of deleterious mutations in tightly linked chromosomal segments that are locally 'sheltered' from purifying selection.
source: The long-term balancing selection acting on mating types or sex-determining genes is expected to lead to the accumulation of deleterious mutations in the tightly linked chromosomal segments that are locally 'sheltered' from purifying selection.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical work (Uyenoyama, 1997; Uyenoyama, 2005) and represents established theoretical predictions in population genetics.

claim: Linkage to the S-locus locally distorts phylogenies over about 10–30 kb along the chromosome.
source: We find that linkage to the S-locus locally distorts phylogenies over about 10–30 kb along the chromosome.
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic analyses presented in Figure 2 and related analyses showing the extent of linkage disequilibrium around the S-locus.

claim: More intense balancing selection on dominant S-alleles results in greater fixation of linked deleterious mutations.
source: The more intense balancing selection on dominant S-alleles results in greater fixation of linked deleterious mutations, while recessive S-alleles accumulate more linked deleterious mutations that are segregating.
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic data presented in Figure 4 showing the correlation between S-allele dominance and fixed deleterious mutations.

claim: Recessive S-alleles accumulate more linked deleterious mutations that are segregating.
source: The more intense balancing selection on dominant S-alleles results in greater fixation of linked deleterious mutations, while recessive S-alleles accumulate more linked deleterious mutations that are segregating.
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic data presented in Figure 4 showing the correlation between S-allele dominance and segregating deleterious mutations.

claim: The structure rather than the overall magnitude of the linked genetic load differs between dominant and recessive S-alleles.
source: Hence, the structure rather than the overall magnitude of the linked genetic load differs between dominant and recessive S-alleles.
evidence: This claim is supported by the combined results showing no difference in total deleterious mutations (Figure 3) but differences in fixed versus segregating mutations (Figure 4).

claim: Self-incompatibility is controlled by a single non-recombining chromosomal region, the S-locus, in the Brassicaceae family.
source: In the Brassicaceae family, SI is controlled by a single non-recombining chromosomal region, the S-locus (Schopfer et al., 1999; Kusaba et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research establishing the genetic basis of self-incompatibility in Brassicaceae.

claim: S-alleles in Arabidopsis lyrata and Arabidopsis halleri are distributed into four classes of dominance, with increasing dominance from class I to class IV.
source: In Arabidopsis lyrata and Arabidopsis halleri, the S-alleles are distributed into four classes of dominance, with increasing dominance from class I to class IV and linear dominance also observed inside some of the classes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Llaurens et al., 2008; Durand et al., 2014) that characterized the dominance hierarchy.

claim: Dominance between S-alleles is controlled by small RNAs molecules produced by dominant S-alleles that target and repress expression of recessive S-alleles in pollen.
source: This system is genetically determined and controlled by small RNAs molecules produced by dominant S-alleles that are able to target and repress expression of the recessive S-alleles in pollen (Durand et al., 2014; Yasuda et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies that identified the molecular mechanism of dominance.

claim: Recessive S-alleles can form homozygous combinations in natural populations more often than dominant S-alleles.
source: Specifically, recessive S-alleles can form homozygous combinations in natural populations more often than dominant S-alleles (Billiard et al., 2007), such that recombination can occur occasionally between distinct gene copies of the same recessive S-allele, providing the opportunity for the linked recessive deleterious mutations to be purged from within the S-locus itself.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to theoretical work (Billiard et al., 2007) predicting the frequency dynamics of S-alleles.

claim: Recessive S-alleles reach higher population frequencies than dominant S-alleles.
source: In addition, because recessive S-alleles reach higher population frequencies (Billiard et al., 2007; Llaurens et al., 2008), purifying selection on linked deleterious variants is expected to have higher efficacy among gene copies of recessive than dominant S-alleles.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical and empirical studies (Billiard et al., 2007; Llaurens et al., 2008).

claim: A significant decrease of Ah03/Ah03 homozygotes at the reproductive stage compared with Mendelian expectations was observed.
source: However, we observed a significant decrease of Ah03/Ah03 homozygotes at the reproductive stage compared with Mendelian expectations (Supplementary file 1a), whereas the observed proportion of the Ah03 S-allele among heterozygous individuals did not depart from expectations (2/3 = 0.67; Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Table 1 showing departure from Mendelian ratios.

claim: The proportion of Ah01/Ah01 and Ah04/Ah04 homozygotes surviving to the reproductive stage was consistent with Mendelian expectations.
source: The proportion of Ah01/Ah01 and Ah04/Ah04 homozygotes surviving to the reproductive stage was consistent with Mendelian expectations in their respective families.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Table 1 showing no departure from Mendelian ratios.

claim: A genetic load was observed linked to the Ah03 S-alleles, which is at an intermediate level of dominance.
source: Thus, the increased mortality is associated with Ah03 homozygosity, rather than with a lower performance of individuals carrying the Ah03 S-allele itself. Overall, a genetic load was thus observed linked to the Ah03 S-alleles, which is at an intermediate level of dominance, but neither to the most dominant (Ah04) nor to the most recessive (Ah01) S-allele.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing differential survival of Ah03 homozygotes.

claim: No effect of homozygosity at the S-locus on variation of the traits measured was found, with a single exception (maximum length of flowering stems).
source: Overall, with a single exception, we found no effect of homozygosity at the S-locus on variation of the traits measured (Figure 1; Supplementary file 1b). The maximum length of flowering stems was the exception to this general pattern, with longer reproductive stems for S-locus homozygous than heterozygous genotypes, hence in the opposite direction from our expectation of lower fitness in homozygotes.
evidence: This claim is supported by phenotypic measurements presented in Figure 1 and Supplementary file 1b.

claim: No effect of S-allele dominance on the contrast between S-locus homozygotes and heterozygotes was observed for any of the measured traits, with one exception (time to produce the first leaf).
source: We also observed no effect of S-allele dominance on the contrast between S-locus homozygotes and heterozygotes for any of these traits. A single of the 13 traits was an exception to this general pattern, but again the effect was in the opposite direction from our expectation, with an earlier rather than delayed appearance of the first leaf for homozygotes of more dominant S-alleles (Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by GLM analyses presented in Supplementary file 1d.

claim: 126 distinct copies of S-alleles were sequenced and phased in two populations of Arabidopsis halleri and three populations of Arabidopsis lyrata.
source: We then sequenced and phased polymorphisms in the chromosomal regions linked to 126 distinct copies of S-alleles in two populations of Arabidopsis halleri and three populations of Arabidopsis lyrata.
evidence: This claim is supported by the description of the sequencing and phasing methodology in the Materials and methods section.

claim: 34 haplotypes linked to 12 distinct S-allele lineages were reconstructed in Nivelle.
source: Overall, we were able to reconstruct 34 haplotypes linked to a total of 12 distinct S-allele lineages in Nivelle, 38 haplotypes linked to 11 distinct S-allele lineages in Mortagne, and 16, 22, and 16 haplotypes associated with 6, 7, and 5 distinct S-allele lineages in populations IND, PIN, and TSS, respectively (Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: This claim is supported by the phasing results presented in Supplementary file 1e.

claim: 38 haplotypes linked to 11 distinct S-allele lineages were reconstructed in Mortagne.
source: Overall, we were able to reconstruct 34 haplotypes linked to a total of 12 distinct S-allele lineages in Nivelle, 38 haplotypes linked to 11 distinct S-allele lineages in Mortagne, and 16, 22, and 16 haplotypes associated with 6, 7, and 5 distinct S-allele lineages in populations IND, PIN, and TSS, respectively (Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: This claim is supported by the phasing results presented in Supplementary file 1e.

claim: Nine S-alleles were shared between the two A. halleri populations (Ah01, Ah03, Ah04, Ah05, Ah12, Ah20, Ah24, Ah25, and Ah59).
source: Nine of the S-alleles were shared between the two A. halleri populations (Ah01, Ah03, Ah04, Ah05, Ah12, Ah20, Ah24, Ah25, and Ah59).
evidence: This claim is supported by the S-allele identification results.

claim: The difference in log likelihood between the two topologies (by S-alleles vs. by populations) decreased significantly with distance to the S-locus.
source: The difference in log likelihood between the two topologies decreased significantly with distance to the S-locus (Pearson coefficient = –0.015 and –0.010 for A. halleri and A. lyrata, respectively; p-values<2e-16).
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic analyses presented in Figure 2B.

claim: In A. halleri, the topology grouping haplotypes by populations became more likely than the topology grouping them by S-alleles at a distance of around 30 kb from the S-locus.
source: In A. halleri, the topology grouping haplotypes by populations became more likely than the topology grouping them by S-alleles at a distance of around 30 kb from the S-locus, but even at a distance of 50 kb the phylogenetic structure was still different from that in regions unlinked to the S-locus used as controls for the genomic background (Le Veve et al., 2023; Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic analyses presented in Figure 2B.

claim: In A. lyrata, the shift from topology by S-alleles to topology by populations occurred within 10–15 kb.
source: In A. lyrata, the shift was even more rapid (within 10–15 kb), although we note that the phylogenetic structure of the control regions was less resolved (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic analyses presented in Figure 2B.

claim: FST values among S-alleles were high in regions close to the S-locus and quickly decreased to reach the background level as the distance from the S-locus increased.
source: In both A. halleri and A. lyrata, FST values among S-alleles were high in regions close to the S-locus and quickly decreased to reach the background level (Figure 2B—figure supplement 8) as the distance from the S-locus increased.
evidence: This claim is supported by FST analyses presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 7 and 8.

claim: Differentiation among populations was initially low in regions close to the S-locus and increased up to background level within the first few kilobases.
source: In parallel, the differentiation among populations followed roughly the opposite pattern, that is, it was initially low in regions close to the S-locus (as expected under strong balancing selection) and increased up to background level within the first few kilobases (Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by FST analyses presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claim: All S-alleles except one were associated with unique SNPs in the 50 kb region around the S-locus.
source: As expected, the vast majority of significant associations were found for the most closely linked SNPs. With a single exception, all S-alleles were associated with unique SNPs in the 50 kb region around the S-locus, albeit with substantial heterogeneity among S-alleles in the patterns and extent of associations that they show (Figure 2—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by association analyses presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 8.

claim: Different S-alleles are associated with specific sets of tightly linked mutations within 10–30 kb.
source: Hence, different S-alleles are associated with specific sets of tightly linked mutations, but only within 10–30 kb.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple analyses including phylogenies, FST, and association studies presented in Figure 2 and related supplements.

claim: No overall effect of dominance on the number of zerofold degenerate mutations (S0f) was found.
source: We found no overall effect of dominance on S0f (p-values = 0.54 and 0.07 for A. halleri and A. lyrata, respectively; Figure 3; Supplementary file 1f) or S0f/S4f (p-values = 0.54 and 0.07 for A. halleri and A. lyrata, respectively; Supplementary file 1f).
evidence: This claim is supported by GLM analyses of genomic data presented in Figure 3 and Supplementary file 1f.

claim: Lineages of dominant S-alleles tend to fix deleterious mutations more readily than recessive S-alleles.
source: In agreement with the prediction of Llaurens et al., 2009b, we observed that lineages of dominant S-alleles do indeed tend to fix deleterious mutations more readily (Figure 4; Supplementary file 1f).
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic analyses of fixed mutations presented in Figure 4 and Supplementary file 1f.

claim: Dominant S-alleles tend to have more fixed deleterious mutations, but recessive S-alleles compensate by accumulating a larger number of segregating mutations.
source: The fact that dominant S-alleles tend to fix deleterious mutations more readily but do not accumulate a larger total number of deleterious mutations is explained by the fact that the structure of the genetic load differs between dominant and recessive S-alleles: the dominant S-alleles tend to have more fixed deleterious mutations, but the recessive S-alleles compensate by accumulating a larger number of segregating mutations, resulting in similar numbers of deleterious mutations overall in most of the populations.
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic analyses presented in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Stochastic simulations confirmed that, at equilibrium, dominant S-alleles tend to accumulate a larger number of recessive deleterious mutations that are fixed among gene copies within S-allele lineages.
source: Our stochastic simulations confirmed that, at equilibrium, dominant S-alleles tend to accumulate a larger number of recessive deleterious mutations that are fixed among gene copies within S-allele lineages (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results presented in Figure 5A.

claim: The number of segregating linked mutations was higher for recessive than for dominant S-alleles in simulations.
source: In contrast, the number of segregating linked mutations was higher for recessive than for dominant S-alleles (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results presented in Figure 5B.

claim: The mean number of linked deleterious mutations per copy of S-allele was not expected to change between dominant and recessive S-alleles in simulations.
source: These two effects eventually compensate each other, such that in the end the mean number of linked deleterious mutations per copy of S-allele was not expected to change between dominant and recessive S-alleles (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results presented in Figure 5C.

claim: The A. lyrata populations colonised North America from ancestral European populations about 20–30,000 years ago.
source: Indeed, the A. lyrata populations colonised North America from ancestral European populations about 20–30.000 years ago (Clauss and Mitchell-Olds, 2006; Ross Ibarra et al., 2008) and are less diverse overall than the A. halleri populations we studied, who colonised the north of France during the last century from ancestral German populations (Pauwels et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on the demographic history of A. lyrata (Clauss and Mitchell-Olds, 2006; Ross Ibarra et al., 2008).

claim: The A. halleri populations studied colonised the north of France during the last century from ancestral German populations.
source: Indeed, the A. lyrata populations colonised North America from ancestral European populations about 20–30.000 years ago (Clauss and Mitchell-Olds, 2006; Ross Ibarra et al., 2008) and are less diverse overall than the A. halleri populations we studied, who colonised the north of France during the last century from ancestral German populations (Pauwels et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study on the demographic history of A. halleri (Pauwels et al., 2005).

claim: S-locus homozygous genotypes formed by crossing individuals carrying identical alleles from distinct populations should not reveal as much load as when they are formed by crossing individuals within populations.
source: The progressive decoupling between alleles and their linked sites leads to the simple prediction that S-locus homozygous genotypes formed by crossing individuals carrying identical alleles from distinct populations should not reveal as much load as when they are formed by crossing individuals within populations.
evidence: This claim is a prediction based on the observation that linked mutations differ between populations, representing a logical inference from the data.

claim: The S-locus region could contribute to overall hybrid vigour.
source: Hence, the S-locus region could contribute to overall hybrid vigour.
evidence: This claim is a speculative inference based on the prediction about reduced load in inter-population crosses.

claim: The most consistent pattern of the sheltered load seems to be a decrease of overall juvenile survival.
source: Hence, the most consistent pattern seems to be a decrease of overall juvenile survival, possibly because it is a highly integrative measurement of fitness, whereas other morphological or life history traits can be associated with more specific components of overall fitness.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of results across multiple studies and represents an inference from the literature.

claim: The magnitude of the S-linked load varied among S-alleles.
source: In line with this prediction, the magnitude of the S-linked load varied among S-alleles as the load linked to some S-alleles was phenotypically detectable, while for others it was not.
evidence: This claim is supported by the phenotypic measurements showing differential effects across S-alleles.

claim: The same suite of linked mutations was consistently associated among different copies of a given S-allele when sampled from within the same population, particularly for dominant S-allele lineages.
source: Also in line with the model of the sheltered load, our phasing of a large number of variants linked to S-haplotypes in several natural populations revealed that the same suite of linked mutations was consistently associated among different copies of a given S-allele when sampled from within the same population, in particular for the dominant S-allele lineages under more intense balancing selection.
evidence: This claim is supported by the phasing and phylogenetic analyses presented in Figure 2 and related supplements.

claim: The association between S-alleles and linked sites was lost when examining sites at increasing genetic distances from the S-locus along the chromosome.
source: As expected for outcrossing populations with short-scale linkage disequilibrium, this association was lost when examining sites at increasing genetic distances from the S-locus along the chromosome (see also Le Veve et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by the phylogenetic and FST analyses showing decay of association with distance.

claim: The association with linked sites was further lost when comparing gene copies of S-alleles sampled from different local populations.
source: Finally, the association with linked sites was further lost when comparing gene copies of S-alleles sampled from different local populations, suggesting that recombination within populations decouples alleles from their linked sites faster than migration can homogenise the genetic composition among these natural populations.
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic analyses showing population structure in more distant regions (Figure 2).

claim: Recombination within populations decouples alleles from their linked sites faster than migration can homogenise the genetic composition among natural populations.
source: Finally, the association with linked sites was further lost when comparing gene copies of S-alleles sampled from different local populations, suggesting that recombination within populations decouples alleles from their linked sites faster than migration can homogenise the genetic composition among these natural populations.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that haplotypes cluster by population rather than by S-allele in distant regions.

claim: The allele Ah15 is one of the most 'loaded' alleles among all the dominant S-alleles present in the Nivelle population.
source: Finally, we note that our genomic analysis of the genetic load shows that the dominant allele Ah15 previously associated with reduced fitness in homozygotes (Llaurens et al., 2009b) is indeed unusual in terms of the number of mutations it carries. In fact, it is one of the most 'loaded' alleles among all the dominant S-alleles present in this population, possibly explaining why Llaurens et al., 2009b observed a significant effect despite the inherently limited experimental power of their analysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic data presented in Figure 3A showing Ah15 has a high number of mutations.

claim: Self-compatible intermediates are expected to be capable of selfing as well as forming homozygous genotypes that would otherwise be prevented.
source: Specifically, the self-compatible intermediates required for the formation of new S-alleles (Gervais et al., 2011; Bergero and Charlesworth, 2009) are expected to be capable of selfing as well as forming homozygous genotypes that would otherwise be prevented.
evidence: This claim is based on citations to previous theoretical work (Gervais et al., 2011; Bergero and Charlesworth, 2009) and represents established knowledge.

claim: In natural populations, self-compatible mutants may segregate more readily for the more recessive than for the more dominant S-alleles.
source: Hence, our results lead to the prediction that in natural populations self-compatible mutants may segregate more readily for the more recessive than for the more dominant S-alleles, and more generally for allelic lineages under lower intensity of balancing selection.
evidence: This claim is a prediction based on the differential structure of the genetic load between dominant and recessive S-alleles.

claim: The diversification dynamics should be more efficient for lineages of recessive than dominant S-alleles.
source: Considering that self-compatible mutants are a necessary intermediate stage in the formation of new S-alleles, one may predict that the diversification dynamics should be more efficient for lineages of recessive than dominant S-alleles.
evidence: This claim is a prediction based on the inference about self-compatible mutants segregating more readily in recessive S-alleles.

claim: The most dominant S-alleles exhibit the deepest phylogenetic divergence among them in Arabidopsis.
source: This prediction is in line with the observation in Arabidopsis that the most dominant S-alleles exhibit the deepest phylogenetic divergence among them (Durand et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Durand et al., 2014) that characterized S-allele phylogeny.

claim: Y or W sex chromosomes accumulate a greater genetic load than X or Z chromosomes, respectively.
source: The classical case of Y or W sex chromosomes are indeed examples where one balanced line accumulates a greater genetic load than the other (X or Z, respectively), eventually leading to substantial genetic degeneration (Wright et al., 2016; Ponnikas et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on sex chromosome evolution (Wright et al., 2016; Ponnikas et al., 2018).

claim: The genetic load on the derived 'Satellite' haplotype is higher than on the ancestral 'Independent' haplotype in the ruff supergene.
source: Another example is the supergene controlling variation in male plumage phenotypes of the ruff, where the genetic load on the derived 'Satellite' haplotype is higher than on the ancestral 'Independent' haplotype (Lamichhaney et al., 2016; Hill et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on the ruff supergene (Lamichhaney et al., 2016; Hill et al., 2022).

claim: In the butterfly Heliconius numata, the inverted haplotypes conferring mimetic wing patterns tend to accumulate a greater load than the non-inverted haplotypes.
source: Similarly, in the butterfly Heliconius numata, the inverted haplotypes conferring mimetic wing patterns tend to accumulate a greater load than the non-inverted haplotypes (Rosser et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study on Heliconius numata (Rosser et al., 2022).

claim: In all cases where one haplotype accumulates greater load, the haplotypes with the greatest load also act genetically in a dominant manner.
source: Interestingly, in all these cases, the haplotypes with the greatest load also act genetically in a dominant manner, establishing a clear parallel with our observations.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on comparison of patterns across multiple systems cited in the text.

claim: The presence of deleterious mutations linked to S-alleles has been shown to affect the evolution of dominance modifiers, favouring evolution towards greater dominance than towards greater recessivity.
source: The presence of deleterious mutations linked to S-alleles has been shown to affect the evolution of dominance modifiers, favouring evolution towards greater dominance than towards greater recessivity (Llaurens et al., 2009a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous theoretical study (Llaurens et al., 2009a).

claim: S-alleles that become recessive will start forming homozygous genotypes, leading to expression of their linked load.
source: This asymmetry arises from the fact that S-alleles that become recessive (e.g. following acquisition of a recessivity modifier such as a small RNA target) will start forming homozygous genotypes, leading to expression of their linked load, while S-alleles that become dominant will not.
evidence: This claim is based on theoretical reasoning about the consequences of changes in dominance.

claim: Many deleterious mutations linked to recessive S-alleles are segregating.
source: Our observation that many deleterious mutations linked to recessive S-alleles are indeed segregating suggests that expression of the load will be less severe for recessive than for dominant S-alleles, hence decreasing this predicted asymmetry.
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic data presented in Figure 4 showing higher segregating mutations in recessive S-alleles.

claim: Expression of the load will be less severe for recessive than for dominant S-alleles.
source: Our observation that many deleterious mutations linked to recessive S-alleles are indeed segregating suggests that expression of the load will be less severe for recessive than for dominant S-alleles, hence decreasing this predicted asymmetry.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that segregating mutations in recessive S-alleles may remain masked in homozygotes.

claim: 399 offspring were obtained from a total of six crosses for the phenotypic experiment.
source: We obtained 399 offspring from a total of six such crosses.
evidence: This claim is a direct statement of the experimental sample size.

claim: The experimental procedure used here differs from that of Llaurens et al., 2009b in that it did not require CO2 treatment to bypass the SI system.
source: Note that our experimental procedure differs slightly from that of Llaurens et al., 2009b in that their procedure required a CO2 treatment to bypass the SI system and obtain selfed offspring, while here we took advantage of the dominance interactions to obtain outcrossed S-locus homozygous individuals that we phenotypically compared to their full-sibs with S-locus heterozygous genotypes.
evidence: This claim describes a methodological difference between studies.

claim: The S-locus homozygous offspring obtained contain distinct gene copies of a given S-allele lineage.
source: Note also that the S-locus homozygous offspring we obtained contain distinct gene copies of a given S-allele lineage. Hence, they could in principle carry distinct suites of linked deleterious mutations in case these mutations segregate within S-allele lineages.
evidence: This claim is based on the experimental design and represents an inference about the genetic composition of the offspring.

claim: The observed proportion of the Ah03 S-allele among heterozygous individuals did not depart from expectations (2/3 = 0.67).
source: However, we observed a significant decrease of Ah03/Ah03 homozygotes at the reproductive stage compared with Mendelian expectations (Supplementary file 1a), whereas the observed proportion of the Ah03 S-allele among heterozygous individuals did not depart from expectations (2/3 = 0.67; Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Table 1.

claim: The increased mortality is associated with Ah03 homozygosity, rather than with a lower performance of individuals carrying the Ah03 S-allele itself.
source: Thus, the increased mortality is associated with Ah03 homozygosity, rather than with a lower performance of individuals carrying the Ah03 S-allele itself.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that heterozygotes carrying Ah03 show normal proportions while homozygotes show reduced survival.

claim: The phenotypic results did not replicate the observation of Llaurens et al., 2009b that dominant S-alleles carry a more severe deleterious load than recessive S-alleles.
source: Overall, our phenotypic results confirmed the presence of a detectable linked load on some phenotypic traits (survival; time to produce the first leaf), but we could not replicate the observation of Llaurens et al., 2009b that dominant S-alleles carry a more severe deleterious load than recessive S-alleles, even though our samples were obtained from the same local population.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of the current phenotypic results with those of Llaurens et al., 2009b.

claim: A total of 4854 variable sites were obtained from the 126 S-locus haplotypes.
source: Altogether, we were able to obtain the phased flanking sequences of 126 S-locus haplotypes, comprising a total of 4854 variable sites.
evidence: This claim is a direct statement of the sequencing results.

claim: Mutations in the S-locus flanking regions can be exchanged between S-alleles by recombination and between local populations by migration.
source: Mutations in the S-locus flanking regions can be exchanged between S-alleles by recombination and between local populations by migration (Charlesworth, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous theoretical work (Charlesworth, 2006) and represents established knowledge.

claim: The relative time scale of recombination vs. migration determines the distribution of the linked mutations.
source: The relative time scale of these two processes (recombination vs. migration) determines the distribution of the linked mutations.
evidence: This claim is based on theoretical reasoning about population genetic processes.

claim: Differentiation between populations started to exceed differentiation between S-alleles much closer to the S-locus in the A. lyrata than in the A. halleri populations.
source: In line with our phylogenetic analysis, differentiation between populations started to exceed differentiation between S-alleles much closer to the S-locus in the A. lyrata than in the A. halleri populations (Figure 2—figure supplements 3–5 and Figure 2—figure supplement 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by FST analyses presented in Figure 2—figure supplements 3-5 and 7B.

claim: Extending the analysis to all non-synonymous mutations or to deleterious mutations predicted by SIFT4G and by SNPeff led to identical conclusions regarding the lack of overall effect of dominance on total deleterious mutations.
source: Extending the analysis to all non-synonymous mutations or to deleterious mutations predicted by SIFT4G and by SNPeff led to identical conclusions (Supplementary file 1f).
evidence: This claim is supported by additional analyses presented in Supplementary file 1f.

claim: The conclusion that dominant S-alleles fix deleterious mutations more readily held true when extending the analysis to all non-synonymous mutations and to the lowly and moderately deleterious mutations predicted by SNPeff.
source: This conclusion held true when extending the analysis to all non-synonymous mutations and to the lowly and the moderately deleterious mutations predicted by SNPeff (Supplementary file 1f).
evidence: This claim is supported by additional analyses presented in Supplementary file 1f.

claim: The simulation predictions are in line with the genomic observations.
source: These predictions are in line with our genomic observations and suggest that the dominance level of S-alleles modifies the structure of the genetic load they shelter: dominant S-alleles accumulate more fixed deleterious mutations, but recessive S-alleles accumulate more segregating mutations, resulting in an equivalent load overall.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison between simulation results (Figure 5) and genomic data (Figures 3 and 4).

claim: The dominance level of S-alleles modifies the structure of the genetic load they shelter.
source: These predictions are in line with our genomic observations and suggest that the dominance level of S-alleles modifies the structure of the genetic load they shelter: dominant S-alleles accumulate more fixed deleterious mutations, but recessive S-alleles accumulate more segregating mutations, resulting in an equivalent load overall.
evidence: This claim is supported by both genomic data and simulation results.
